_about: College placements after SFFA (stage 04). Every number was checked against its source on 2026-11-21. Quotes in notes are verbatim. A record with verified false or value null renders as a placeholder.

charts.title: Fall 2023 to fall 2025: how many elite colleges went down
charts.measure: Number of the 27 elite colleges in Bloomberg's analysis

records.metric: Elite colleges with a smaller share of Black first-year students in fall 2025 than in fall 2023
records.source: Liam Knox and Francesca Maglione, "College Diversity Drops Again as Trump Ramps Up Scrutiny," Bloomberg Law, Jan. 14, 2026
records.notes: Article text: 'In a Bloomberg analysis of data from 27 elite schools, all but two reported a smaller share of Black freshmen in fall 2025 than in fall 2023, the last class admitted before the affirmative action ban.' 25 = 27 minus 'all but two'. The visible text does not name the 27 schools.

records.metric: Elite colleges with reduced Hispanic first-year enrollment, fall 2023 to fall 2025
records.source: Liam Knox and Francesca Maglione, "College Diversity Drops Again as Trump Ramps Up Scrutiny," Bloomberg Law, Jan. 14, 2026
records.notes: Article text: 'Some 21 schools saw reduced Hispanic enrollment among first-year students over that period.' Bloomberg says 'enrollment' here, not 'share' as it does for Black students, and does not say which. The same article: 'more than half the schools reported equal or higher Asian enrollment in the 2025 freshman class compared to 2023.'

stats.metric: Elite institutions reporting fall 2025 data where Black enrollment fell
stats.caption: elite institutions reporting fall 2025 data saw Black enrollment fall.
stats.data_year: Fall 2025 entering classes; comparison year not stated
stats.source: Julie J. Park, "Is Race-Conscious Admissions Really Dead?" Higher Education Today (American Council on Education), Apr. 13, 2026, citing James S. Murphy's post-SFFA enrollment tracker
stats.notes: Article text: 'Out of 29 elite institutions reporting data for fall 2025, Black enrollment fell at 24 and Latino enrollment fell at 16.' The article does not say which year it compares to or whether 'enrollment' means share or count. Its data link is Murphy's tracker, which reports shares and uses the average of the 2022 and 2023 classes as its baseline. This is a different, larger set of colleges than Bloomberg's 27, so the two counts are not directly comparable.

supporters.label: What supporters of the ruling argue
supporters.quote: Eliminating racial discrimination means eliminating all of it.
supporters.who: Chief Justice John Roberts, for the majority

source.cite: SFFA v. Harvard, opinion of the Court, slip op. at 15

outcome.label: What the outcome data shows
outcome.text: At {bloomberg-black-share} elite colleges, Black students made up a smaller share of the fall 2025 first-year class than of the fall 2023 class. A separate count found Black enrollment down at {ace-29-black} elite institutions reporting fall 2025 data.

cascade.illustrative_note: The dots are illustrative, not counts. No verified source gives flows between tiers, so none are shown.

tier_source.notes: Paper: highly selective colleges are "those with pre-pandemic acceptance rates below 25%"; selective "25-60%"; less selective "above 60%".

why.text: In fall 2024, the first year after the ruling, high-achieving Black, Hispanic, Native American and Pacific Islander students were less likely to enroll at highly selective colleges and more likely to “cascade” into less selective ones, which have lower graduation rates and earnings outcomes. For this site’s pipeline, that can mean fewer students reaching a CS degree at stage 05 and a tech job at stage 06.

sources.cite: JBHE on James S. Murphy’s Class Action report

research.metric: Change in likelihood of enrolling at a highly selective college, fall 2024 vs. fall 2023
research.display: Up to 10 percentage points (about 14%) less likely
research.data_year: First entering class after SFFA (fall 2024) vs. fall 2023; 12.6 million domestic PSAT, SAT and AP takers in the 2021-2024 graduation cohorts linked to National Student Clearinghouse enrollment
research.source: Bloem, M. D., Edwards, A., Goyer, J. P., Howell, J., Hu, X., Hurwitz, M., Imlay, S. J., Ma, J., & Pender, M. (2026). College enrollment patterns after SFFA v. Harvard (EdWorkingPaper No. 26-1392). Annenberg Institute at Brown University
research.notes: Abstract: "high-achieving underrepresented minority (URM) college-goers were up to 10 percentage points (14 percent) less likely to enroll in highly selective colleges in fall 2024 than fall 2023, with URM enrollees cascading down the college selectivity distribution into less selective colleges with lower graduation rates and earnings outcomes." URM = Native American, Hispanic, Black or Pacific Islander. The data come from College Board and the National Student Clearinghouse; the paper says it reflects the authors’ views, not theirs.

research.metric: URM share of first-year domestic students at highly selective colleges, first year after SFFA
research.data_year: Fall 2024, difference-in-differences estimate using earlier state bans
research.source: Bloem, M. D., Edwards, A., Goyer, J. P., Howell, J., Hu, X., Hurwitz, M., Imlay, S. J., Ma, J., & Pender, M. (2026). College enrollment patterns after SFFA v. Harvard (EdWorkingPaper No. 26-1392). Annenberg Institute at Brown University
research.notes: Abstract: "we estimate that the URM student share of first-year domestic students at highly selective colleges declined 4 to 5 percentage points (18 percent) in the first year after SFFA, with smaller declines at selective public colleges."

research.metric: Where students went in fall 2024, across more than 3,000 colleges
research.group: Class Action report by James S. Murphy
research.source: "New Report Analyzes Post-Affirmative Action Enrollment Outcomes at Over Three Thousand U.S. Institutions," The Journal of Blacks in Higher Education, Feb. 9, 2026
research.notes: Murphy, quoted by JBHE: the ruling "created, at least in its first year, a cascade effect in which highly qualified students of color who would have been much more likely to be admitted to highly selective institutions" ended up "enrolling in less selective institutions." JBHE also reports "a slight increase in Black freshman enrollment at institutions with lower graduation rates and expected earnings post-graduation" and Black freshman enrollment up 30% at LSU and 50% at the University of Mississippi. The AOL link in the brief returned 404; it appears to reprint a story from The Hill that could not be opened, so its figures are not used.

other_side.intro: Supporters of the ruling and some researchers read the same enrollment data differently. Here is what they argue, in their own words where possible.

positions.quote: noticeable, though modest, racial demographic shifts
positions.quote_lead: Using IPEDS data on more than 1,000 four-year colleges from 2010 to 2024, the report finds the most selective colleges saw
points: It asks whether some colleges’ warnings to the Court “prove[d] overstated.”
It says a lack of demographic change “does not necessarily indicate noncompliance,” and calls for more scrutiny where warranted and more admissions transparency.
positions.figure: At Ivy League schools, Black enrollment fell from about 11% to 8% and Hispanic from 16% to 15%, while white rose from 35% to 37% and Asian from 30% to 32%.

source.cite: "New Report: Students for Fair Admissions Decision Reshapes Elite College Enrollment," Manhattan Institute, May 14, 2026

positions.notes: Press release text, verbatim: "VerBruggen finds that the most selective colleges experienced noticeable, though modest, racial demographic shifts"; "At Ivy League schools, Black enrollment fell from about 11% to 8%; Hispanic enrollment fell from 16% to 15%; white enrollment rose from 35% to 37%; and Asian enrollment rose from 30% to 32%." The release frames the question as whether "some institutions’ warnings to the Court prove overstated". The full report is linked from the release; the before and after years for the Ivy figures are not stated in the release.

positions.quote: the highly qualified students of color who lost an advantage in the admissions process due to SFFA were not going to opt out of higher education altogether
points: Black enrollment fell at highly selective colleges, but total Black enrollment at four-year institutions held steady as more students enrolled at less selective schools.
More than four of five state flagship universities enrolled more underrepresented students of color in 2024.

source.cite: "Black enrollment shifts, not shrinks, after affirmative action ban: report," The College Fix, Feb. 27, 2026

positions.notes: College Fix: "total black enrollment at four-year institutions held steady due to increased participation at less selective schools, according to a new report from Class Action"; "more than four of five state flagship universities had increases in enrollment of underrepresented students of color in 2024." Murphy also notes that enrollment data alone cannot show intent or compliance. The report date is not given; JBHE covered it on Feb. 9, 2026. The "January 2026 report" in The College Fix is Richard Sander’s separate law school study, not Murphy’s.

positions.who: Robert Steinbuch, University of Arkansas, with Richard Sander, UCLA
positions.quote: It’s clearly positive to see a reordering of admissions to place students where they will best thrive.
points: Their “mismatch hypothesis” holds that students admitted with much weaker credentials than their classmates may do worse than they would at a less selective school.
Sander’s January 2026 study of law schools found Black and Hispanic enrollment did not fall overall; it shifted toward less selective schools.

source.cite: "Black enrollment shifts, not shrinks, after affirmative action ban: report," The College Fix, Feb. 27, 2026

positions.notes: Steinbuch quote and the mismatch description are from The College Fix. The mismatch hypothesis is contested; the article notes that Yale scholars Ian Ayres and Richard Brooks have objected to it. Sander’s study covers law schools, not undergraduate admissions.

other_side.synthesis: Both sides agree on the core numbers above: fewer Black students at the most selective colleges. They disagree on what the shift means. Supporters see students landing where they fit; the national study in this section finds the less selective colleges they land at have lower graduation rates and earnings.
